sentences.text: 10. In the present case, mother of victim Adarsh namely Priti, PW-1 and PW-2 (inadvertently mentioned as PW-1) Priyanka, who are the surviving victims of the accident, have testified as an eye witnesses.
Both have categorically asserted that the accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the offending truck.

Though their allegations have been denied by the insurance company by way of cross-examination, there is no denial of the occurrence of the accident or involvement of the offending vehicle or even the allegations of rash and negligent driving by Respondent no.1 himself, in his written statement.
Further, merely because the accident was a head-on collision, no inference as to the joint fault of both the involved vehicles can be drawn.

Also, in as much as, the site plan reveals the accident to have occurred close to the center of the road, without any clarification from either parties or the investigation officer as to if such road was divided by a concrete divider or merely divided by a marking line, no adverse presumption can be raised against the driver of the Ecco car for having driven his vehicle in proximity to the dividing lines.
With no evidence to the contrary led by the insurance company or other respondents, such Ecco car is assumed to have been in its permissible lane.

Even if four minor passengers allegedly travelling in the said car are ignored to have caused overloading or excess weight, the presence of other nine adult passengers (including the driver) in the car would still be considered as a traffic violation.

However, before such traffic violation can be equated to contributory negligence, the concept of contributory negligence may be analysed through the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Pramod kumar Rasikbhai Jhaveri Vs. sentences.text: Subject to non-requirement of the existence of duty, the question of contributory negligence is to be decided on the same principle on which the question of defendant's negligence is decided.
The standard of reasonable man is as relevant in the case of plaintiff's contributory negligence as in the case of defendant's negligence.
But the degree of want of care which will constitute contributory negligence, varies with the circumstances and the factual situation of the case.

The following observation of the High Court of Australia in Astley v. Austrust Ltd.1 is worthy of quoting:
"A finding of contributory negligence turns on a factual investi-gation whether the plaintiff contributed to his or her own loss by failing to take reasonable care of his or her person or property.
What is reasonable care depends on the circumstances of the case.
In many cases, it may be proper for a plaintiff to rely on the defendant to perform its duty.
But there is no abso-lute rule.
The duties and responsibilities of the defendant are a variable factor in determining Charu by Charu gupta gupta 2025.12.17 18:09:19 +0530 MACT No:124/21 Adarsh (minor)v. Sant Prakash & ors.
P.No. 7 of 23 BK whether contributory negligence exists and, if so , to what degree.

In some cases, the nature of the duty owed may exculpate the plaintiff from a claim of con-tributory negligence; in other cases, the nature of the duty may reduce the plaintiffs share of responsibility for the damage suffered; and in yet other cases the nature of the duty may not prevent a finding that the plaintiff failed to take reasonable care for the safety of his or her person or property.
Contribu-tory negligence focuses on the conduct of the plaintiff.

The duty owed by the defendant,
although relevant, is one only of many factors that must be weighed in determining whether the plaintiff has so conducted itself that it failed to take reasonable care for the safety of its person or property."

14. Drawing an analogy from these decisions, in the present case, no causal connection or nexus between the overloading of Ecco car and the accident has been established by any of the respondents.
It is pertinent to note that the driver of the offending vehicle has nowhere pleaded that the Ecco car was not hit by his vehicle or that it met with an accident solely due to disbalancing.

The impact of head-on collision of an Ecco car with a heavy vehicle such as a truck in the present case,

sentences.text: The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.

The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.

This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.

P.No. 5 of 23 BK in Parmeshwari vs. Amir Chand & Ors., 2011 (1) SCR 1096 and National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana, 2009 ACJ 287, wherein it has been held that the negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view has to be taken.
Both have categorically asserted that the accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the offending truck.
Though their allegations have been denied by the insurance company by way of cross-examination, there is no denial of the occurrence of the accident or involvement of the offending vehicle or even the allegations of rash and negligent driving by Respondent no.1 himself, in his written statement.

Also, in as much as, the site plan reveals the accident to have occurred close to the center of the road, without any clarification from either parties or the investigation officer as to if such road was divided by a concrete divider or merely divided by a marking line, no adverse presumption can be raised against the driver of the Ecco car for having driven his vehicle in proximity to the dividing lines.
With no evidence to the contrary led by the insurance company or other respondents, such Ecco car is assumed to have been in its permissible lane.
However, before such traffic violation can be equated to contributory negligence, the concept of contributory negligence may be analysed through the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Pramod kumar Rasikbhai Jhaveri Vs. The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner.
The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable.
A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury.
This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.
It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii),
